accessibility-violations.title: Accessibility Violations
accessibility-violations.description: A newsletter sign-up form full of deliberate accessibility problems, with a switch to a fixed version, for practising automated and manual accessibility checks.

information.summary: Every accessibility problem on this page is deliberate. Switching on Show the fixed version (or opening #/accessibility-violations?version=fixed) fixes all of them, so the same scan can be run against both versions. Each problem is listed under Expected problems, below.

sections.title: Running the scan
points: The problems are all inside the Newsletter sign-up section, whose ID is accessibility-violations-area.

Limit the scan to that section, so nothing from the rest of the playground mixes in: .include('#accessibility-violations-area') in @axe-core/playwright or cy.checkA11y('#accessibility-violations-area') in cypress-axe.
Each row under Expected problems has a data-rule attribute with its rule ID (or data-issue for the keyboard problems), and the table empties in the fixed version.

sections.title: What makes it tricky to automate
points: duplicate-id-aria is reported under incomplete rather than violations, because axe-core marks the rule as needing review, so a test that only looks at violations never sees it.
heading-order is a best practice rather than a WCAG rule, so a scan limited with withTags(['wcag2a', 'wcag2aa']) misses it.
color-contrast and scrollable-region-focusable depend on how the page is laid out, so they are only found in a real browser and never in jsdom.
One rule can fail on several elements and new axe-core versions add rules, so assert on the rule IDs you expect rather than on the number of violations.

sections.title: What a scanner cannot find
points: The Message box keeps the Tab key for itself, the way some code editors indent, so once it has focus neither Tab nor Shift+Tab leaves it: a keyboard trap.
The Subscribe button is a div with a click handler, so it cannot be reached with Tab and only works with a mouse.
A clean scan does not prove a page is accessible: it only shows that the problems a scanner can find are gone.

actionability.title: Actionability
actionability.description: Overlays, moving buttons, layout shift and elements that are present but cannot safely be clicked.

information.summary: Every element on this page is in the DOM and looks clickable, but a real click on it either misses or hits something else. This is where errors like "element click intercepted", "element is not stable", "element is outside of the viewport" and "element does not receive pointer events" come from. The Last action panel at the top shows what each click actually hit.

sections.title: Covered elements
points: In the Overlays section, the Accept terms button is covered for good by a transparent element, so the click is always intercepted: the test should report that rather than pass with a forced or JavaScript click, which would hide a bug a user would hit.
The Continue button is covered by a transparent loading overlay for a few seconds after the page loads, so a test has to wait for it to clear, not sleep for a fixed time.
The sticky header sticks to the top of the window while you scroll through the product list, so a tool that scrolls a button to the top of the window before clicking it will click the header instead.

sections.title: Elements that move
points: In Moving elements, one button never stops moving, so a stability check never passes and a click at its old position misses; the other moves for a few seconds and then settles, so waiting for it to be stable works, and the Last action panel says whether you clicked it while it was moving.

In Layout shift, a banner is injected above Confirm order a couple of seconds after the page loads and its Upgrade to premium button lands exactly where Confirm order was, so a click that worked out its position too early upgrades instead of confirming.

sections.title: Out of view or not clickable
points: The I agree button is inside a scrollable box rather than the page, so the box itself has to be scrolled before the button is in view.

One button has pointer-events: none, so the pointer passes straight through it, and another has no width or height at all, so it is in the DOM with text but is not visible. Clicks on both only work through JavaScript, which is not what a user can do.

sections.title: Matching and markup
points: The input follows the ARIA combobox pattern: aria-expanded says whether the list is open and aria-activedescendant points at the highlighted option, which has aria-selected="true".
Suggestions match anywhere in a name, ignoring case and accents, with names that start with what you typed listed first, and the matching part is in bold.

broken-images-and-links.title: Broken Images and Links
broken-images-and-links.description: A gallery and a list of links where some work and some do not, including a 404 image, an image with an invalid URL, a lazy-loaded image, missing pages and anchor links.

information.summary: Some of the images and links on this page work and some do not, for checking that every image loads and every link leads somewhere. Each image and link has a data-expected attribute of ok or broken, so a test can compare what it finds with what it should find.

sections.title: Broken images
points: A broken image is still in the page: it keeps its src, shows its alt text and is visible, so checking that the <img> exists or is visible passes. Check that it has finished loading and has a size instead: img.complete && img.naturalWidth === 0 means it failed.
The image with an invalid URL never makes a request at all, so it does not show up as a 404 in the network log. Only the image itself tells you it failed.
Listening for failed responses only catches requests made after the listener is added, so add it before loading the page.

sections.title: Lazy loading
points: The last image has loading="lazy" and sits below the fold, so the browser does not request it until it is scrolled near the viewport.

Until then complete is false and naturalWidth is 0, so a check that runs straight away reports it as broken (or, with Check images, as not loaded yet). Scroll it into view and wait for it to load before checking it.

sections.title: Checking links
points: Clicking every link is slow and leaves the page, so request each URL with an API request instead (page.request.get() in Playwright, cy.request() in Cypress) and check the status is below 400. Read the resolved href property rather than the attribute, which may be relative.
A missing static file, such as the old gallery page, returns a real 404.

This playground uses hash routing, so a link to a page in the app such as #/cookies-and-storage only requests the home page: the server returns 200 even for a page that does not exist. Open these links and check the page shows its content instead.
External sites may block automated requests, rate limit them or be down, which makes external link checks flaky. Many suites check them on a schedule rather than on every run.

sections.title: Anchor links
points: Because the # in the URL is already used for routing, the links to sections on this page are handled by script: clicking one scrolls to the section without changing the URL.
To check an anchor, look for an element whose id matches the part after the #. The link to the reviews section has no matching section, so clicking it does nothing.

canvas-and-svg.title: Canvas and SVG
canvas-and-svg.description: A drawing pad, a bar chart and a target game drawn on canvas, and an SVG map with hover tooltips, where what is shown cannot be found with normal DOM queries.

information.summary: Nothing drawn on a canvas is in the DOM: the bars, the target and your drawing are only pixels, so there is no element or text for a locator to find. A test has to act at coordinates and check the results written underneath each canvas. Every canvas is shown at the size it is drawn at, so a position in CSS pixels from its top left corner is the same position in canvas pixels: use click({ position: { x, y } }) in Playwright or .click(x, y) in Cypress.

sections.title: Drawing pad
points: A stroke needs the button pressed, the pointer moved and the button released, so a single click draws nothing and is not counted.
Drive it with page.mouse.move, page.mouse.down and page.mouse.up, which use page coordinates, so add the position of the canvas's bounding box, or trigger pointer events on the canvas.
The number of strokes and points is shown under the pad and in its data-strokes and data-points attributes.

sections.title: Bar chart
points: The canvas is 480 × 260 pixels, bar i (counting from 0) is 50 pixels wide and centred at x = 75 + 70 × i, and the axis is at y = 230, so clicking at y = 225 always hits a bar.
A click between or above the bars says no bar was clicked.

sections.title: Target
points: The target has a radius of 15 pixels and appears at (60, 60), (340, 240), (200, 150), (320, 50) and (80, 250), in that order.
Its current centre is in the canvas's data-target-x and data-target-y attributes, a shortcut a real game would not give you.

sections.title: District map
points: The map is SVG, so its regions are elements, but they have no role or accessible name and the svg is a single image to assistive technology, so role-based locators find nothing inside it.
Find a region with [data-region="harbour"]. XPath needs //*[local-name()='polygon'], because SVG elements are in their own namespace.
The Harbour wraps around the Old Town, so the middle of its bounding box, where tools click and hover by default, is in the Old Town: click it with an offset, for example near its bottom edge.

The names on the map ignore the mouse and pass clicks to the region underneath, so a tool that checks which element is under the pointer before clicking, as Playwright does, waits for a name to receive the click and times out.
The tooltip only appears while the mouse is over a region and follows it, so it needs a hover rather than a click.

sections.title: Screenshot tests
points: Everything is drawn at a fixed size in fixed colours, whatever the theme, with no animation and nothing random, so the same actions always give the same picture.

Take the screenshot of just the canvas or the map rather than the whole page, and expect small differences between browsers, operating systems and fonts (anti-aliasing and text): keep a baseline for each browser and platform, or allow a small threshold.
The pixels can also be read directly with canvas.toDataURL() or getContext('2d').getImageData().

challenging-selectors.title: Challenging Selectors
challenging-selectors.description: Random IDs, identical buttons, split text and hidden duplicates that break naïve selectors.

information.summary: This page is built so that the obvious selectors fail. The Last action panel at the top shows what your last click actually did, so you can check you hit the element you meant to.

sections.title: IDs and order that change
points: The IDs and class names in the first section (and the class names elsewhere) are random hashes, like those from CSS-in-JS libraries, and change every time the page loads, so find the field by its label and the buttons by their role and name instead.

The team table is shuffled on every load and every row has the same Edit and Delete buttons with no accessible name of their own, so pick the row by its content (the person's name or email) and then the button inside that row; a row position or nth match will hit someone else.

sections.title: Split text
points: The greeting and unread message count are split across several elements, so a match on an element's own text will not find the whole sentence: match on the text of the parent, or normalise the text first.
The marking button's label is split the same way, but its accessible name is still the full sentence.

sections.title: Missing labels
points: The two address blocks have fields whose labels are plain text that is not tied to the inputs, and the two blocks are identical apart from their title, so you have to locate a field relative to the nearby text or by its position inside the right block.

The two newsletter forms do the same thing: the labelled one has a heading, a label, a real button and data-testid attributes, while the unlabelled one only has a placeholder, a clickable div styled like a button and random class names, so compare how each locator strategy copes with both.

sections.title: Duplicate elements
points: The Checkout button is in the page three times: a mobile and a desktop version, of which only one is shown depending on the screen width, and a third inside the closed More options panel, so a locator has to target the visible one rather than the first one in the DOM.

clipboard.title: Clipboard
clipboard.description: Copy values to the clipboard, read it back and see how pages can change or block a paste.

information.summary: Reading and writing the system clipboard needs permissions that are not part of the page, and every browser handles them differently, so grant clipboard-read and clipboard-write in your test framework (where it supports them) and check the result by reading the clipboard back rather than trusting the Copied! label.

sections.title: Permissions and browsers
points: The Clipboard API only exists in a secure context (HTTPS or localhost) and must be called from a user gesture while the page has focus, so a click from a test that has moved focus elsewhere can still fail.

In Chromium, grant clipboard-read and clipboard-write (in Playwright with context.grantPermissions), or reading is refused with a permission error. Firefox and WebKit do not support these permissions in the same way: Firefox shows its own Paste pop-up for readText, which a test cannot click.
Headless browsers may use a clipboard of their own that is not shared with the operating system, and tests running in parallel on one machine can overwrite each other's clipboard in headed mode.
If permission is denied or the API is missing, the page shows an error explaining which, so the failure is easy to spot in a screenshot.

sections.title: Copying
points: Each Copy button writes its value with navigator.clipboard.writeText and reads Copied! for two seconds. Assert on what the clipboard holds, not only on the label.
The API key is shown masked but the full key is copied, so the text on screen is not what ends up on the clipboard.

sections.title: Pasting
points: Paste from clipboard reads the clipboard with navigator.clipboard.readText and shows what it found.

The notes field cancels the paste event and inserts a cleaned-up, plain-text version, so typing the text, setting the value or simulating a paste each gives a different result. A synthetic paste event needs a clipboardData holding text/plain.
The Confirm password field rejects pasted text, so a test that fills it by pasting fails and must type the password instead. Filling the field directly skips the paste event altogether.

sections.title: Blocked copying
points: The second reference field cancels the copy and cut events, so selecting its text and pressing the copy shortcut leaves the clipboard unchanged. Compare it with the field next to it.

cookies-and-storage.title: Cookies and Storage
cookies-and-storage.description: Answer a cookie consent banner, save cookie preferences, keep a note for this tab only, and watch the cookies and storage change.

information.summary: Almost every real site shows a cookie consent banner on the first visit, and it covers the page until it is answered, so it is the first thing that gets in the way of an end-to-end test. Here the banner only appears a second after the page loads, the way banners added by a third-party script do, so checking that it is not there straight after the page loads passes too early.

sections.title: Where the state is kept
points: The choice is remembered in the cookie_consent cookie (accepted, rejected or custom), and the analytics and marketing choices are kept in localStorage under cookie_preferences, so both survive a reload.
The session note is kept in sessionStorage, which belongs to a single tab: it survives a reload but is gone in a new tab or a new browser context.

sections.title: Keeping tests independent
points: Tests that share a browser context leak this state into each other, so start each test with a clean context, or use Clear everything.

Clicking through the banner in every test is slow and brittle; instead, seed the state before the page loads, with context.addCookies, page.addInitScript or a saved storageState in Playwright, or cy.setCookie and onBeforeLoad in Cypress, as shown at the bottom of the page.

sections.title: Inspecting and clearing storage
points: The live view only reads storage when this page changes it, so after changing storage from a test, press Refresh or reload the page.
Clear everything only removes what this scenario stores; the playground's own language and theme settings are kept.

date-picker.title: Date Picker
date-picker.description: A custom calendar date picker: single dates, disabled days, a date range and a field you can type into or pick from.

sections.title: Navigating the calendar
points: Each picker opens its calendar in a popup that is added at the end of the page's <body>, not next to its field, so look for it from the whole document rather than inside the field's container.
There is no typing into the appointment or trip pickers: to reach a date in another month, use the previous and next month buttons or the month and year lists, and check which month is showing first.
The trip picker stays open after the first day and closes after the last; picking a day before the first starts again from there.
In the calendar the arrow keys move by day and week, Page Up and Page Down by month, Home and End to the start and end of the week, Enter picks the focused day and Escape closes it.

sections.title: Which days can be picked
points: Which days can be picked depends on today's date, read from the browser's clock when the page opens, so a test that picks "next Monday" or "the 15th of this month" gets a different date (or a disabled one) on a different day unless the clock is faked.
Disabled days are still shown and can be focused, but they are marked aria-disabled, struck through, and clicking them does nothing.
Appointments and trips can be booked up to the end of {{lastYear}}.

sections.title: Reading the chosen date
points: Each day is a button whose text is just the day number, whose accessible name is the full date in the current language (e.g. "Friday, November 20, 2026") and which has a data-date attribute in ISO format.
Under each picker the chosen value is shown in ISO format (YYYY-MM-DD), the same in every language: assert on that rather than on the displayed text.

sections.title: Differences between languages
points: The date of birth field follows the current language's format (MM/DD/YYYY in English, DD/MM/YYYY in French and Portuguese), so 03/04/2000 is 4 March in English but 3 April in French, and the text is only checked when Enter is pressed or the field loses focus; dates in the future or before {{minYear}} are refused.
The week starts on Sunday in English and Portuguese and on Monday in French, so the same date is in a different column.

sections.title: The dropdowns
points: The first two are native <select> elements, so most frameworks can choose an option directly by its value or text; the second allows several options to be picked at once.

The third is a custom dropdown built from buttons and a list: it is not a <select>, and its options only exist in the DOM, at the end of the page, while it is open, so click it to open it and then click an option.
Some options are disabled and cannot be picked.

dynamic-loading.title: Dynamic Loading
dynamic-loading.description: Elements that appear, disappear and change state after a random delay.

information.summary: Each section changes the page after a random delay of between {{min}} and {{max}} seconds, picked again every time, so a fixed sleep is sometimes too short and always slower than needed: wait for the condition you actually need instead.

sections.title: Each section
points: The first section adds an element to the DOM only once its spinner finishes, so it cannot be found before then.
The second has its element in the DOM from the start but hidden with display: none, so it is present long before it is visible.
The third has an input that is disabled until the async step finishes, and clicking it while disabled does nothing.
The fourth removes its checkbox and later adds a brand new one, so a reference to the old element goes stale and has to be looked up again.
The last shows "Loading..." and then "Still loading..." before its final text, so waiting only for "Loading..." to go away is not enough: wait for the text you expect.

hovers.title: Hovers
hovers.description: Interact with elements that only appear while the mouse is over something.

information.summary: Everything on this page only shows up while the mouse pointer rests on something, so tests have to hover first. The last thing you did is shown underneath.

sections.title: Each section
points: The details on each profile card are not in the DOM at all until the card is hovered, and on purpose there is no other way to reveal them.

The buttons on each file are always in the DOM but stay invisible until their row is hovered, so a test that clicks them straight away will be told they are not visible; keyboard users can also reveal them by tabbing to the row.

The rich text editor works like many classic WYSIWYG editors: the text you edit is the body of a frame, while its toolbar, word count and HTML output are on the page around it, so a test has to move between the two.

information.summary: Everything on this page is driven by the keyboard, so tests have to send key presses rather than click or type text. There is no mouse alternative on purpose.

sections.title: Each control
points: The key reader shows the last key pressed in its text box, with its key and code and any modifier keys held with it, plus the last few keys pressed.

The counter only changes while it has focus: the up and down (or right and left) arrow keys move it by 1, holding Shift moves it by 10, Home and End jump to the lowest and highest values and Escape puts it back where it started.
The hold control only confirms if Space is held down for a whole second; letting go sooner does not count, and holding a key down repeats its keydown event, so each repeat has to be ignored.

modal-dialogs.title: Modal Dialogs
modal-dialogs.description: Open, use and close dialogs drawn in the page, including one that appears by itself on load.

sections.title: Finding a modal
points: Unlike the browser's native dialogs (see JS Alerts), these modals are ordinary DOM elements, but each is rendered in its own element at the end of <body>, outside the scenario's markup, so look for it from the document rather than inside the section that opened it.

While a modal is open a full-screen backdrop sits over the page and everything behind it is marked inert and aria-hidden="true": clicks on the page are intercepted by the backdrop and background elements drop out of the accessibility tree, so role-based queries no longer find them.

sections.title: Each modal
points: The basic modal closes with its close button, the Escape key or a click on the backdrop, and reports which one was used.
The confirmation modal guards a delete: the safe Cancel button gets focus, and Escape or the backdrop also cancel.
The form modal keeps focus trapped inside while it is open (Tab wraps around) and gives focus back to the button that opened it when it closes.
The stacked modals show a second dialog on top of the first: Escape and the backdrop only close the top one.

sections.title: The welcome modal

sections.title: Each target
points: The double-click target ignores single clicks and only counts double-clicks.

The note opens a custom context menu on right-click instead of the browser's own one, and its items pin, highlight or delete the note; the menu is a separate element positioned where the pointer was, and it closes on Escape or when you press anywhere outside it.

The hold button only confirms if the left mouse button is held down on it for a whole second, so the press and release have to be sent as separate steps with a wait in between; letting go or moving off it sooner does not count, and the progress bar shows how far through the hold you are.
The last box reports which mouse button was pressed (left, middle, right, back or forward) and which modifier keys (Shift, Control, Alt, Meta) were held at the time.

multi-step-form.title: Multi-Step Form
multi-step-form.description: A sign-up wizard spread over several steps, with per-step validation, a step that only appears for business accounts, an optional step, a review page with edit links, and answers that survive a reload. The current step is kept in the URL.

information.summary: The form is split into steps: personal details, company details (business accounts only), address, preferences (optional) and a review. Each step has its own URL, such as ?step=address, and answers are saved in sessionStorage as you go.

sections.title: Steps and the URL
points: Next adds a history entry, so the browser's back button goes back a step, just like the form's Back button.

A step can only be shown once every step before it is finished. Opening ?step=review on a fresh page lands on the first step instead, and the URL is corrected with history.replaceState. Wait for the URL or the step heading to settle rather than asserting straight after navigating.

To deep-link to a later step, either fill in the earlier steps through the UI, or seed the multi-step-form key in sessionStorage before the page loads, for example with page.addInitScript() in Playwright or onBeforeLoad in Cypress. The data must be valid and the earlier steps listed as completed (or skipped, for the optional step).

sections.title: Validation and conditional content
points: Next only checks the fields on the current step. Errors appear after Next is clicked, then update as you type, and focus moves to the first field with an error.
Back does not validate, so a finished step can be left invalid. Going forward again, or opening a later step's URL, brings you back to it.
Choosing Business adds a company details step, so the step count changes from 4 to 5 and every later step moves up by one. Find steps by name or by the data-step attribute, not by their position.
The preferences step is optional: Skip moves on without saving it as completed, and the review shows it as skipped. The phone number field only exists while Phone is the chosen contact method.
Switching back to a personal account hides the company step. Its answers are kept, but no longer shown on the review.

sections.title: Review, focus and saved answers
points: Every section on the review has a link whose visible text is just Edit. Their accessible names say which step they open, for example Edit Address, so look them up by role and name. After an edit, the main button reads Save and return to review instead of Next.
When the step changes, focus moves to the step's heading. Typing straight after clicking Next types into nothing.

Answers survive a reload but not a new tab or a new browser context, as sessionStorage belongs to one tab. Start over, or clear the storage, so tests do not see each other's answers. Submitting clears them too.

Each step is a natural page object, with a shared component for the progress list and the Back, Next and Skip buttons, and the steps map well onto BDD scenarios such as Given I have filled in my personal details.

paginated-table.title: Paginated Table
paginated-table.description: Find invoices across the pages of a table with search, filters, row selection and a bulk action.

information.summary: The table holds 143 invoices, shown 10, 25 or 50 at a time. The summary, dates and amounts are worded and formatted differently in each language.

sections.title: Loading
points: Every change (a new page, page size, search or filter) loads for a random {{min}} to {{max}} ms, and while it loads the old rows stay on screen: the table is marked aria-busy="true", an overlay with a spinner covers it and the pager, page size and checkboxes are disabled.
Checking the rows straight after a click can read the old page, so wait for the load to finish or for the row count summary to change.

sections.title: Searching, filtering and paging
points: The search box only searches once typing has paused for {{debounce}} ms, and then loads again; it matches the invoice number or the customer, ignoring case and accents ("cafe" finds "Café Étoile").
A new search, filter or page size goes back to page 1, and both ends of the date range are included.
The pager shows the first and last pages and those either side of the current one, with … for the rest, so the page you want may not have a button yet; the current page is marked aria-current="page".
When nothing matches, the table shows a message with a button to clear the filters, and the pager is removed.

sections.title: Selecting rows
points: Selected rows stay selected when you change page or filter, even when they are no longer shown, and the selected count includes them.
The checkbox in the header only selects the rows on the current page, and is partly checked when only some of them are.
Marking invoices as paid changes them straight away, so with a status filter on they can disappear from the page.

shadow-dom.description: Elements hidden inside open, nested and closed shadow roots, so you can check how your tools reach into the shadow DOM.
shadow-dom.information: Regular selectors stop at a shadow root boundary. The open shadow root can be pierced by most tools, the nested example needs two hops, the slotted content lives in the light DOM even though it is shown inside a shadow root, and the closed shadow root cannot be reached through host.shadowRoot at all.

sortable-table.title: Sortable Table
sortable-table.description: Sort a table by clicking its column headers.

information.summary: Click a column header to sort by it: the first click sorts ascending, the second descending and the third puts the rows back in their original order. The current sort is shown underneath the table.

sections.title: What to look out for
points: The sorted column's header says which way it is sorted in its aria-sort attribute, and the other headers have none; the Email column cannot be sorted.

The values are picked to catch naive sorting: salaries and project counts sort wrongly as text, start dates are shown in your language's format, one name starts with an accented letter, and several people share a department (they keep their original order when tied).
The contractor has no salary and always sorts last, whichever way the column is sorted.

time-and-timers.title: Time and Timers
time-and-timers.description: A countdown offer, an inactivity timeout, relative timestamps, time-of-day content, a debounced search and a throttled button.

information.summary: Everything on this page depends on the current time or on time passing, and the waits are deliberately long: the offer runs for five minutes, and the session warning only appears after ten minutes without any activity.

sections.title: Controlling the clock
points: Waiting for them in real time makes a test slow and flaky, so take control of the clock instead, with page.clock in Playwright, cy.clock() and cy.tick() in Cypress, or vi.useFakeTimers() in Vitest.
Install the fake clock before the page loads, because timers started before it are left on the real clock.

The page re-reads the clock every second and works out every state from the current time, so jumping the clock forward (for example with page.clock.fastForward(), which fires a due timer only once) lands on the right state straight away.

sections.title: What depends on the clock
points: The greeting and the opening hours banner depend on the time of day and the day of the week, so a test that does not fix the time passes or fails depending on when it runs: set a fixed time such as a Saturday, or a weekday at 08:00, before loading the page. They also use the browser's time zone.
The relative timestamps move from "just now" to "1 minute ago" and on to hours and days, and their exact time is in the datetime attribute.

sections.title: Session timeout
points: The session timeout counts any mouse movement, click, key press or scroll as activity, so a test that moves the mouse while waiting resets it.

The warning covers the whole page, so while it is showing every other click on the page is intercepted until it is dismissed; once the warning is showing only Stay signed in keeps the session, and once signed out only Sign in again starts a new one.

sections.title: Search and save
points: The search only runs once you stop typing for half a second, so a test should wait for the results, or advance the clock, rather than check them straight after typing; the counter under the search box shows how many searches actually ran.
Save is throttled: after a save, further clicks for two seconds are ignored, so clicking it twice in quick succession only saves once.

virtualised-list.title: Virtualised List
virtualised-list.description: Lists of 10,000 rows and a grid of 260,000 cells where only the rows on screen exist in the DOM. Rows are created, reused and removed as you scroll.

information.summary: Each list has 10,000 rows and the grid has 260,000 cells, but only the handful near the viewport are in the DOM. The count above each list shows how many rows are rendered right now and which ones, so you can watch them change as you scroll.

sections.title: Rows off screen do not exist
points: Looking for row {{fixedTarget}} straight away finds nothing: it is not hidden, it is simply not in the DOM yet. scrollIntoView() cannot help either, as there is no element to call it on. Scroll the list itself (not the page) until the row is rendered, then find it.

Counting rows with getAllByRole('listitem'), locator.count() or should('have.length') gives the number rendered, not the total. The real totals are in aria-setsize on each row, and aria-rowcount and aria-colcount on the grid.
Searching the page for text, with getByText or the browser's find, only sees the rendered rows.

In the DOM does not mean on screen: a few extra rows are rendered above and below the viewport so fast scrolling does not show gaps. Playwright scrolls a rendered row into view before clicking it; elsewhere check it is visible first.

sections.title: Elements are reused
points: As you scroll, the element that showed one row is reused for another: the element that showed row 3 may show row 18 after a scroll. A stored element, such as a Selenium WebElement or a Cypress alias, can point at a different row afterwards without going stale, so find the row again after every scroll.

Find rows by something that belongs to the row, such as its text, its data-row-id or its button's name (Select row {{fixedTarget}}), not by position: nth() or eq() picks the nth rendered row, not the nth row of the list.
Each row's Select button has the same visible text, so a locator for the text alone matches whichever rows are rendered.

sections.title: Scrolling to a row
points: In the fixed-height list every row is {{rowHeight}}px tall, so row N starts at (N - 1) × {{rowHeight}} pixels. Set the list's scrollTop to that and the row is rendered.

In the variable-height list rows have different heights, so a row's position cannot be worked out from its ID. Scroll a step at a time, for example by the height of the list, and after each step check whether the row is rendered. The IDs of the rendered rows tell you whether to keep going or go back.

Rows are rendered in response to the scroll event, so wait for the row to appear rather than checking straight after scrolling. Setting scrollTop, mouse.wheel() in Playwright and scrollTo() on the list in Cypress all fire it.

The grid scrolls both ways: its columns are virtualised too, so column Q is not in the DOM until you scroll right. Its header row and row numbers stay in place over the cells, so a cell scrolled just under them is in the DOM but covered.

multiple-file-upload.title: Multiple File Upload
multiple-file-upload.description: Choose several files at once, and add images through a drop zone with a hidden input, type and size checks, previews, a progress bar per file and remove buttons.

information.summary: The first section is a native file input that takes several files at once. The second is a drop zone, as most upload widgets are built: the real input is hidden, files are checked as they are added, and each one uploads with its own progress bar.

sections.title: The input behind the drop zone
points: The drop zone's <input type="file"> is visually hidden and out of the tab order: users only see the zone and its Browse files button. Playwright's setInputFiles() works on hidden inputs, so target #drop-zone-input directly. Cypress's selectFile() checks the element is actionable, which a hidden input can fail, so pass { force: true }.

Clicking Browse files opens the operating system's file dialog, which no test tool can drive. In Playwright, wait for the filechooser event and call setFiles() on it; elsewhere skip the click and set the input's files.

To test the drop itself, simulate one on the zone. In Cypress use selectFile(file, { action: 'drag-drop' }) on the zone. In Playwright, build a DataTransfer in the page with page.evaluateHandle() and pass it to dispatchEvent('drop', { dataTransfer }). Selenium has no built-in way, so run a script that dispatches the events.
The input is emptied after every selection, so the same file can be chosen again after removing it. Checking the input's files therefore tells you nothing: check the list of files instead.

sections.title: Choosing several files
points: The first input has the multiple attribute. Pass an array to setInputFiles() or selectFile(). In Selenium, send the absolute paths to sendKeys() joined by newlines.
Choosing again replaces the selection rather than adding to it, as native inputs do, whereas the drop zone adds to its list every time.
Files do not have to exist on disk: Playwright takes { name, mimeType, buffer } and Cypress takes { contents, fileName, mimeType }.

sections.title: Validation
points: Only PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP images up to {{max}} each are accepted. The input's accept attribute only filters the file dialog: files set by a test or dropped get past it, so the page checks every file itself and lists the ones it turned away.

The type is taken from the file's MIME type, not its name, so a file called photo.png with the type text/plain is rejected. Set the MIME type yourself when building files in a test, or it is guessed from the extension.

A file with the same name and size as one already in the list is rejected as a duplicate. When a selection mixes good and bad files, the good ones are added and only the others are listed in the error.
Testing the size limit needs a file over {{max}}: build one in memory, for example with Buffer.alloc(1024 * 1024 + 1).

sections.title: Progress, previews and removing
points: Each image starts uploading as soon as it is added, and larger files take longer, up to about 3 seconds. Wait for data-status="uploaded", the Uploaded text or the progress bar's aria-valuenow reaching 100, not for a fixed time.
Submit is disabled while any image is still uploading.

Every file has its own remove button named after it (Remove photo.png), and removing works mid-upload too. Find a file's row by its name and act inside it rather than by its position, as removing a file moves the ones after it up.
Previews use blob: URLs made in the page, so their src changes on every run. Check the preview's alt text, or that it loaded (naturalWidth above 0), rather than its src.

tabs-and-accordions.title: Tabs and accordions
tabs-and-accordions.description: Switch between tabs and expand or collapse accordion sections, some of which keep their hidden content in the page and some of which remove it.

information.summary: Tabs and accordions hide content without removing it, or remove it without warning, so a test has to know whether it is checking that something exists or that it is visible, and the clearest way to tell what is open is the ARIA state (aria-selected, aria-expanded) rather than styling.

sections.title: Visible or present
points: The product tabs keep every panel in the DOM and hide the others with the hidden attribute, so a hidden panel's text can still be found: assert on visibility (toBeVisible), not only on presence.

The report tabs render only the selected panel, so the other panels do not exist at all, and anything typed into a panel is lost when you switch away and back. In the product tabs, typed notes survive.
Collapsed accordion sections stay in the DOM, hidden, in the same way as the product tabs.

sections.title: ARIA state and roles
points: Locate tabs and panels by role (tab, tabpanel) and name, and check the selected tab with aria-selected="true". Each panel is labelled by its tab through aria-labelledby.
Accordion headers are buttons inside headings, with aria-expanded and aria-controls pointing at a region labelled by its header.

The Archive tab is disabled with aria-disabled rather than the native disabled attribute, so it can still be clicked and focused but does nothing. Some tools treat aria-disabled as disabled and refuse to click it; others click it happily.

sections.title: Keyboard
points: Only the selected tab is in the tab order (a roving tabindex). Pressing Tab moves from the tab list into the panel, not to the next tab.

<kbd>ArrowLeft</kbd> and <kbd>ArrowRight</kbd> move between tabs and wrap around, <kbd>Home</kbd> and <kbd>End</kbd> go to the first and last, and the disabled tab is skipped. Moving focus also selects the tab.

sections.title: Timing and the URL
points: The Reviews tab takes about 1.5 seconds to load the first time it is selected, showing a loading message with aria-busy until then. Wait for the reviews themselves rather than a fixed delay.
The selected tabs are kept in the URL (?product=reviews&report=monthly), so a test can open a tab directly. An unknown or disabled tab falls back to the first one.
The native <details> disclosures have no aria-expanded: check the open attribute instead. Their content is hidden by the browser, not by the page.
